stories.body:
‘We think dialogue is a good thing,’ Australian PM says after German chancellor urges the US to work with Europe for peace in Ukraine

Australia has endorsed this week’s historic summit between Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin in China, even as European leaders warn that the US president must not make major concessions over the war in Ukraine.

The three-way summit is planned to take place in Shenzhen, where the leaders will gather for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) meeting. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , has warned the talks must not lead to a redistribution of influence among world powers or the abandonment of his country, more than four years into the war sparked by Putin’s full-scale invasion.

Speaking in Manila on Sunday, the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese , welcomed the talks taking place but insisted the clear message to Putin was that the war should end.

Albanese, in the Philippines before a meeting of Quad leaders and talks with south-east Asian leaders at the Asean summit, left open the possibility of joining an Apec group photo with Putin if China wished for it to go ahead.

“We think that dialogue is a good thing and we await the outcome of that dialogue,” he said.

“It’s obviously quite significant, the fact that President Trump will be at Asean as well as at Apec, and that we’ll have a Quad leaders meeting as well.

“We want to see something constructive come out of that, including we want to see a de-escalation in the conflicts around the world.”

German’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz , expressed hesitation about the talks at a meeting of EU leaders on Friday.

“I want to state our message to the US very clearly once again: please, no surprises,” he said. “Stay on Team Europe and Team Ukraine , and let us work together for a genuine peace in Ukraine.”

France’s president, Emmanuel Macron , warned against forcing “an unjust peace” on Ukraine and, by extension, all of Europe.

“That is the spirit of defeat,” Macron said. “That is a recipe for another war.”

The meeting has been compared to a 1945 summit at Yalta , in southern Crimea, when then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin carved up influence across war-ravaged Europe. Zelenskyy has warned that the meeting must not turn into “Yalta 2, 3, 4”.

The historian Timothy Garton Ash has called the trilateral summit, organised after a proposal by Putin last month, “a sort of parody” of Yalta, even as analysts say decisions on the future of Ukraine or China’s ambitions to take control of Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Albanese said the summit would not undercut a growing push by countries including Australia and Canada for middle powers to have greater influence in world affairs.

“We’ll continue to engage with like-minded countries,” he said. “There are two super powers in the world.

“What’s important about the struggle of the people of Ukraine is that they’re not just standing up for their own sovereignty; they’re standing up for the international rule of law.”

Asked if he would join the so-called “family photo” of Apec leaders if Putin took part, Albanese said he would consider the wishes of China as the host nation. But he said the Russian president should know Australia’s opposition to the invasion.

“If he’s in a room where I am, I’m sure they’ll hear my contribution,” Albanese said.

After the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting, Australia’s Penny Wong joined with European and Canadian counterparts to avoid a group photo . It was cancelled by US officials when a third of participants declined to stand alongside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.

Albanese signed a new defence agreement with the Philippines on Sunday, visiting the supply ship HMAS Stalwart in the Port of Manila. Australia is helping to strengthen the Philippines’ defensive capability against Chinese aggression.

More freedom-of-navigation naval exercises are planned in an attempt to counter Beijing’s efforts to influence the South and East China seas.

stories.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
stories.summary: COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
COVID-19 lockdowns cut global fire activity by 12.3 percent.

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Untangling humans from the weather

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without big fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

Weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

The double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

Sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

A natural experiment in staying home

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

The results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Controlling for weather factors was important in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

The 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang said, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”

Not every fire went quiet

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

There are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

One line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires showed a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Understanding the human Impact

Wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

Cell Reports Sustainability, 2026. DOI: 10.1016/j.crsus.2026.100860

stories.title: Suspected China spy linked to Nvidia's ex-boss left in 2025, Megaspeed says
stories.summary: The Nvidia scandal has raised questions over whether advanced AI chips ended up in China, despite US restrictions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
The Nvidia scandal has sent shockwaves through Silicon Valley as well as the political establishment

Published 6 hours ago

Alice Huang, a suspected China spy who has been linked to Nvidia's former boss Jensen Huang, left her executive role at Megaspeed in August last year, the company says.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the AI chip-making giant Nvidia after it emerged he had allegedly had affairs with Alice Huang as well as with one of his employees.

Megaspeed is the biggest buyer of Nvidia chips in south-east Asia and the scandal at Nvidia has raised questions about the possibility that high-end AI chips may have ended up in China despite US export restrictions.

The Singapore-based company said on Sunday it had launched an internal investigation into its business.

It said it was aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

It added that it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

On Friday, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed fellow Trump cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick's commerce department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-end chips.

Bessent told CNBC that several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months... but Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process".

The so-called entity list restricts US trade with overseas firms and individuals.

Lutnick has been called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over his department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Megaspeed is suspected of giving backdoor access to Nvidia chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.

Nvidia has been banned from selling its advanced chips to China.

While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.

Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.

Megaspeed said it "designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes". It said this includes "US export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate".

China has denied that Alice Huang is a spy and warned the US not to use the scandal as a "pretext for imposing a technological blockade" on AI technology.

stories.body:
Long-awaited final report will call for benefit cuts but lack of entry-level jobs is also driving the crisis

‘I’m scared about my future’: young people on the stress and desperation of jobseeking

A generation is being sold short. Almost a million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet). Austerity and the Covid pandemic cast a lengthy shadow, AI is upending the jobs market, and the cost of living is soaring – all under the microscope of the social media age.

On Tuesday, Alan Milburn’s final report on young people and work will bring Britain to a fork in the road: either continue on this path of state and market failure or sharply change direction.

It will be a big test for Andy Burnham’s government. Milburn will call for controversial benefit cuts for under-25s in exchange for a legal guarantee of a job or training. Alongside changes to education and health, his plan will take a decade to implement.

Behind his argument is a principle Labour has struggled with – that restricting benefits to encourage work is a good idea.

The system clearly is not working. Milburn makes the case eloquently – pointing out that for every £1 spent on job support £25 goes on benefits. But there are also important caveats: change will count for nothing unless employers play their part; half of all Neets are not on benefits, and bad jobs and a lack of entry-level opportunities are far bigger drivers of Britain’s youth jobs crisis than the generosity of the benefits system.

Last week, the Bank of England deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told me Britain’s young people were bearing the brunt of a “low-gear economy” , with employers freezing recruitment amid the war in the Middle East.

Unemployment among the under-25s has risen at the fastest rate since the 2008 financial crisis to reach its highest level relative to the total for all ages since the early 1990s. Young people now make up about 40% of all unemployment.

All of this compounds a drop in entry-level jobs over the past two decades. The Saturday job died long ago, while to make matters worse, those positions at the start of the career ladder are most at risk of automation or replacement by AI.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, the places in Britain with the fewest job vacancies have the highest Neet rates. Highlighting stark regional divisions, young jobseekers in Rotherham face a sixfold gap in opportunity relative to their peers in the Cotswolds.

The preferred fixes called for by employers are tax cuts, looser regulations, and holding back rises in the youth minimum wage. But while policy costs are unquestionably a factor to consider, and the state could do more to help young people get ready for work, the problems go much deeper.

When Milburn’s report comes out, corporate Britain will be out in force to show willing. Amazon, Marks & Spencer, Shell and Pret a Manger are among those who have already spotted the PR opportunity to showcase their efforts. But most are doing nowhere near enough.

Of course it costs time and money to run youth outreach programmes, work experience schemes and to help recruits who need support to get up to speed – especially in tough economic times. But the consequences from not doing so are becoming increasingly clear.

Almost half of jobseekers under 25 surveyed by the organisation Youth Employment UK think employers were unsupportive. Stories of the applications black holes and the catch-22 of companies demanding experience – even for entry-level roles – are all too commonplace.

In Britain’s youth jobs crisis, issues with the quality of work on offer and opportunities for progression also play a part. Low paid, insecure jobs are rife – most notably in places with the highest Neet rates. Over the past quarter of a century in-work poverty has increased. Among working households, the relative poverty rate is almost a fifth (18%) compared with 13% in the mid-1990s.

Figures this month show people’s job satisfaction has dropped to the lowest level recorded by the British Social Attitudes survey. Among young people it is particularly gloomy: separate figures show most believe that not everyone can go as far as their talent and hard work will take them.

after newsletter promotion

Young people are more likely to find insecure work , only to end up jobless again within weeks. More than one in 10 are on zero-hours contracts. For many that flexibility is welcome and can be launchpad to a career – a point seized on by employers’ groups. But despite the gig economy boom of the past 25 years, Britain’s Neet rate has only fallen below 10% once.

Countless studies show badly paid and insecure work is linked to poor mental wellbeing . Across all types of jobs, almost 1 million people in Britain suffer from work-related stress, depression or anxiety . But those in poor-quality employment are up to three times more likely to leave the workforce than those in the highest-quality positions.

For the growing number of Neets grappling with mental health problems the prospect of entering a labour market like this is daunting.

Milburn’s view is that, despite these challenges, emphasising participation is unequivocally the right thing to do. With extra support the barriers to work could be overcome.

The argument is getting a job is better than life sitting in a bedroom doomscrolling . Work can give structure, routine, social connects, status and – here’s hoping – some financial security. On the flipside, unemployment is a killer for wellbeing and financially ruinous.

For those who reach the age of 24 without ever having had a job, even if they successfully re-enter the labour market, they stand to lose up to £300,000 in lifetime earnings.

Like most people, the young want to work. Across society as few as 4% of working-age adults say they would ideally prefer not to – dropping to just 2% of under-25s.

But fixing the social contract will require more than benefit cuts and a 10-year overhaul of the state. There is a big job, too, for employers.

Watch: Pat McFadden refuses to rule out that some young people might lose benefits

Published 15 November 2026, 10:56 GMT

The work and pensions secretary has backed the idea that the government should legally guarantee young people help to get into employment.

Pat McFadden told the BBC that job support should be given a "legislative underpinning", adding the level of assistance on offer was currently "vague".

McFadden also confirmed that some current benefit claimants would see their current entitlement to benefits reduced when they are reassessed.

But his Conservative counterpart Helen Whately said the idea of legally guaranteeing support "doesn't make sense" and ministers should focus instead on reducing taxes paid by employers.

It comes ahead of a long-awaited review by former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn, which will recommend on Tuesday that under-25s should be guaranteed job placements or training to help them find permanent work.

His report is also expected to say that under-25s should no longer be able to claim the health element of UK-wide universal credit - or personal independence payment (Pip), the main disability benefit in England and Wales.

Some could be eligible for a new "additional cost allowance" to cover day-to-day costs related to health conditions, under the plans.

Speaking to Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Milburn said the government should divert money away from the benefits system to boost work support, adding he wanted to see "billions" extra spent on help over the next decade.

However, the idea of reducing the entitlement of existing benefit claimants could prove controversial among Labour MPs, who scuppered a previous benefits-cutting plan under Sir Keir Starmer last year.

Milburn said the reduced entitlement for some should be accompanied by a new "duty on government" to provide jobs support to young people, such as apprenticeships, college places, job coaching, or a job.

He added that the temporary nature of previous job support schemes, including the Kickstart programme during the Covid pandemic, meant that they had been less effective as reducing long-term joblessness.

How the new guarantee would work in practice is not yet clear, with McFadden adding it would have to be "carefully" drafted.

Although local councils have some specific legal duties, including in the areas of child protection and homelessness, duties on central government currently tend to be much broader, such as operating a "comprehensive" health service.

This video can not be played

Watch: Helen Whately says legal guarantee of work or training for under-25s 'doesn't make sense'

Asked on the same programme whether he agreed with the idea of a guarantee, McFadden said: "I do think we need some legislative underpinning to this."

He added that the offer of support "needs to be more firm," adding: "People need more certainty about what they are entitled to."

He confirmed that the government planned to move younger claimants onto a new benefits system when they undergo scheduled reassessment, and some of them would not receive "what they would get today".

Other claimants, such as those with long-term disabilities, would receive an increased amount, he added.

Also speaking to Kuenssberg, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said her party backed moves to reduce welfare spending.

But she criticised the proposed legal guarantee of work support, arguing it might "sound a nice thing to do," but ministers would be better off reducing taxes and regulations on businesses to help youngsters find "real jobs".

She added it was "absurd" the government had increased taxes for employers in order to "subsidise things that look like jobs". She added: "Just stop doing the taxing.

Elsewhere in his interview, former health secretary Milburn said:

a sustainable reduction in welfare spending cannot be achieved in two or three years, warning that "crude cuts" to the benefits system would create other additional costs for government

GPs should not be responsible for signing sick notes declaring people unable to work

ministers should "look very carefully" at Labour's manifesto commitment to phase out the reduced minimum wage for those aged 18-21, adding that moves towards this had "imposed a lot of cost" on firms

It comes as the government announced it will further widen eligibly for its scheme that offers jobless under-25s subsidised six-month job roles on the minimum wage.

From next April, eligible claimants will be offered a role after 12 months of unsuccessfully looking for work, rather 18 currently.

It is the second time that eligibility for the scheme has been widened, after the maximum age was increased from 21 to 24 earlier this year .

stories.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
stories.summary: Cost and access barriers are pushing people to modified use and unapproved versions.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Cost and access barriers are pushing people to modified use and unapproved versions.

GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That’s around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.

Modified use of GLP-1 medications was particularly common among those using compounded versions of GLP-1 medications. Among all GLP-1 users, at least 23 percent used a compounded version; an additional 9 percent said they didn’t know whether their GLP-1 was compounded or not.

Potential risks

These versions of GLP-1 drugs are made by compounding pharmacies and are intended to mimic a medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration, such as Wegovy or Ozempic. But compounded drugs themselves are not approved by the FDA; the regulatory agency does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they’re sold. While compounded drugs are considered more accessible and affordable, they generally have higher rates of preparation errors, contamination, and other manufacturing problems compared to non-compounded drugs.

Among people who used these unapproved, potentially riskier GLP-1s, 62 percent were not taking them as prescribed. That’s compared to just 36 percent of GLP-1 users who took brand-name drugs.

The potential risks of taking unapproved GLP-1 drugs at all or taking them in unapproved ways may be missed by users, the CDC researchers note. A 2025 study assessing websites selling compounded GLP-1 medications found that nearly 40 percent of sites stated or implied the drugs were FDA-approved, making it harder for consumers to differentiate the compounded versions from FDA-approved ones. Further, nearly 80 percent of sites used brand names in their advertising, which could further mislead consumers. The researchers noted that using brand names violated FDA regulatory standards.

“Given the substantial use of compounded GLP-1 medications, understanding the safety and quality of compounded GLP-1 medications is an important public health consideration,” the authors conclude. They also call for more research on the common modifications people are using, such as dose and frequency adjustments, saying the data on the safety and effectiveness of these real-world practices “could help guide the development and implementation of clinical guidelines and support appropriate medication use.”

stories.body:
Tussle for influence as trade, tech and regional security to take centre stage in China, Philippines and Cambodia meetings

World leaders will fly in to Asia for back-to-back high-level summits this week against the backdrop of the tussle for influence between the superpowers China and the US.

Beijing will have the home advantage when it welcomes Donald Trump to its southern technology hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) leaders’ meeting. It starts two weeks after the US leader lost midterm elections .

The summit also comes after an awkward-at-best revelation that the head of Nvidia, the US chipmaker that for a long time was the world’s most valuable company, was having an affair with a woman US intelligence suspects was a Chinese spy .

Apec represents more than 60% of global GDP and has primarily promoted free trade and multilateralism. This year’s meeting could be defined, however, by the confirmed trilateral meeting between Trump, the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The three-way meeting has been likened to a modern-day Yalta, when in 1945 then US president, Franklin D Roosevelt, Britain’s Winston Churchill and the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to carve up Europe after the second world war. However, analysts say a “Yalta 2.0” that issues edicts on Ukraine and Taiwan without their involvement is unlikely.

Xiaoyu Pu, an associate professor at the University of Nevada’s department of political science, said a three-way meeting “might be more symbolic than substantive, although symbolism itself matters in great-power diplomacy.

“Trump appears interested in nuclear arms control and denuclearisation. Xi’s priority is likely to maintain a stable relationship with Washington while preserving China’s strategic partnership with Russia. Putin, meanwhile, wants to maintain his bargaining leverage over Ukraine.”

Apec begins on Wednesday and follows a flurry of other diplomatic gatherings, chief among them the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) meeting in the Philippines , starting on Sunday, which Trump will attend.

While he is in Manila, US officials will hold a sidelines meeting of the so-called Quad – Australia, India, Japan and the US. In addition, a Francophone summit, which includes the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, and the French president, Emmanuel Macron, is happening concurrently in Cambodia.

Critical global issues at all these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition. Trump’s focus has been on denuclearisation. A key regional focus will be on the South China Sea , where Beijing has built massive military outposts in disputed waters, as well as the gigantic Indonesian forest fire haze blanketing the region.

The humanitarian and security crisis in Myanmar has become a perennial issue, as is status of Taiwan, which China does not recognise. The self-ruled island is sending the founder of the tech hardware company Acer as its envoy to Apec.

Global pivots towards Asia

For well over a decade, Washington’s engagement in the region has been coloured by concern over the rise of China, with the then president Barack Obama telling Australia’s parliament in 2011 that the US was “a Pacific power, and we are here to stay” – a policy known as the “pivot to Asia”.

The strategy of intense diplomacy and trade deals was adopted by Joe Biden, who hoped to gather allies on the continent who wanted to balance their relationships with both superpowers.

Some analysts see Trump’s transactional style in Asia as a continuation of the pivot policy. Still, the president’s volatility and unpredictability have spooked smaller nations, who regard China as a more predictable partner.

Jayant Menon, an economist at Singapore’s Iseas-Yusof Ishak Institute, said that countries in south-east Asia had been “laying the groundwork for a future with reduced dependence on the United States” by seeking deals elsewhere, including with each other and the EU.

“Amid persistent uncertainty and an administration determined to levy tariffs by any legal means, south-east Asia’s ability to ride out another round of tariffs depends on deeper regional integration and diversification beyond the US market,” he wrote this month in the East Asia Forum.

Beijing’s more predictable policies do not necessarily make it any more palatable for its regional neighbours, however, and the Chinese premier, Li Qiang, could have tough talks when he goes to Manila for the Asean summit, especially on the South China Sea.

China’s top diplomat, Wang Yi, recently urged Manila to rein in Filipino politicians who he said had repeatedly “smeared” Beijing, after public outcries in the country over the disputed waters.

Brunei, China, Malaysia, the Philippines, Taiwan and Vietnam have been locked in decades-long territorial standoffs in the busy waterway, which could sit on deposits of oil and gas . Washington has sent military ships on “freedom of navigation operations”, despite Chinese outcries, although US-linked crises in Iran, Ukraine, Venezuela, and Palestine and Israel have sucked up Washington’s focus under Trump’s second term.

A decades-long attempt to sign a South China Sea pact is not expected to happen at this year’s Asean summit, as previously hoped. Despite monthly meetings, negotiations will have to continue next year, when Asean’s leadership rotates to Singapore .

Diplomats at the Asean summit will also be focusing on Myanmar, which is seeking reintegration . Each country in the group is assessing how to deal with their isolated neighbour. The timing of summits this week coincides with a judgment in the international court of justice on Thursday that could find Myanmar responsible for genocide. The coup leader, Min Aung Hlaing, remains barred from Asean but is allowed to send a representative.

Asia’s week of diplomacy will be followed next month by the G20 summit in Miami, Florida, which Xi is expected to attend if US and Chinese relations continue to hold steady.

stories.title: UK ethics watchdog chief steps back from role over sexual misconduct claims
stories.summary: The government says Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role after claims made during the early 2000s emerged.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Stuart Sterling was appointed chief executive of the Ethics and Integrity Commission last year

Published 14 November 2026

The head of the government's main ethics watchdog has stepped back after it emerged he was investigated in a previous job over alleged sexual misconduct involving female colleagues, and had, in one case, been sanctioned.

Stuart Sterling was appointed as the first chief executive of the newly formed Ethics and Integrity Commission in October 2025.

The existence of the allegations against Sterling, and the investigations into them, were first reported by the Sunday Times.

Following the report, a government spokesperson said: "These are serious allegations. Stuart Sterling has stepped back from his role while we swiftly establish the facts."

The Labour Party promised in its 2024 manifesto to create the commission to "ensure probity in government" in response to scandals during the Covid pandemic.

As its head, Sterling's role included advising the prime minister on tackling misconduct in public life.

The Sunday Times reported that, in 2003, Sterling had been subject to a "full misconduct hearing" when he was a junior officer with Northamptonshire Police in what was treated as a case "of sexual harassment".

The paper said he had been accused of inappropriately touching the breasts of a female colleague in a police station, and a male colleague who allegedly witnessed the event had reported him to his superiors. It reported that he had been suspended on full pay.

A representative for Mr Sterling said: "Stuart states that a full disciplinary process was held regarding the complaint in 2002. He complied with this fully. It resulted in a sanction."

The Sunday Times reported that he was given a financial penalty of two weeks' pay. It said that, at the time, that was the maximum sanction possible short of forced resignation. He then received two police commendations and was promoted to be a detective sergeant.

The Sunday Times said that by 2008 Mr Sterling had been reported to the force again after another allegation of sexual misconduct against a female colleague, this time at a social gathering outside work.

Mr Sterling's representative said: "He denies that the alleged incident in 2008 ever took place. He was never subject to any criminal investigation, but the allegation was examined by professional standards".

The representative added: "He was not required to resign from the force. He left voluntarily".

Northamptonshire Police has confirmed that it holds a digital record of a misconduct process from 2002.

It did not comment on the later allegation.

In 2009, Sterling joined the Cabinet Office. It is not clear what vetting process he underwent. He has since served in a variety of senior roles and in 2019 was seconded to the National Police Chiefs' Council. In 2023 he received an OBE for helping to plan the funeral of Queen Elizabeth.

It is understood the Cabinet Office will now examine whether appropriate and correct disclosures of information were made.

stories.summary: Privacy, which companies were once happy to claim was all about personal choice, is now primed to affect everyone around you even more than it already did. Meta and Google’s smart glasses can record anything the owner is looking at or use artificial intelligence to describe it. Apple’s* Audio Intelligence feature turns every Apple Watch into a transcription machine that records or summarizes your day. Amazon’s Bee devices take that a step further and can record and transcribe everything. Dozens of other companies are introducing pendants , rings , and other products designed to record, transcribe, or summarize everything we say and do all day long. Privacy has always been a team sport. The actions you take with communication apps , collaborative software , or your cloud backup solutions , have long impacted everyone else you’re interacting with. But moving those choices deeper into the physical world where strangers, colleagues, family, and friends are all now a part of your privacy choices is drastically changing the game. Tech companies want us to accept a reality where one person’s privacy choices (or lack thereof) means you suddenly need to be an expert in consumer tech who understands the capabilities of many devices on the market, how they work, how and if they signal when they’re recording, and what platforms they do or do not connect to. They believe these ambient surveillance devices that work in the background and are designed to look as normal as possible are the future, while they also expect the owners of these devices to use them responsibly and to notify those around them of their capabilities to act within whatever laws their states may have. This is not reasonable, nor how consent works in any practical sense. stories.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. Named simply Arcade , it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP. ‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

Pill told the Financial Times: “My view would be, we will see evidence that motivates further rises,” adding that the central bank would “do ‌what is necessary to get inflation back to 2% through time”.

The chief economist is one of a number of the Bank’s policymakers who believe the UK economy has gained in strength over the last year, handing workers the power to bid up wages.

Recent figures showed the economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter , to give an annual rate of growth that was only surpassed by the US among the G7 group of wealthy countries.

after newsletter promotion

With inflation expected to rise to 5% in spring next year, driven by high oil and gas prices as a result of the Iran war, Pill expects public and private sector workers to demand substantial pay rises, which would keep inflation high for a longer period.

Pill said he considered an end to the US-Israeli ‌conflict with Iran and a fall in energy prices to be a “very low probability”, indicating that he was poised to vote for another ​quarter-point increase next month.

“My bias, for what it’s worth, is that I worry about the inflationary impact being magnified by second-round effects,” he said, adding that he believed the central bank should have acted sooner to combat inflation. “In my ⁠view, we waited too long.”

While the Bank has not seen evidence of wage increases or companies being able to pass on higher costs to consumers, Pill said the absence of evidence was not evidence of absence.

“As we go into next year, we will begin to see some evidence, and it could play out in one direction or another – we’ll see.”

Financial markets expect UK interest rates to rise to almost 5% in 2027. Pill said these expectations were “not outrageous”, hinting that he could vote for more substantial increases in the cost of borrowing at the next meetings of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) because the “ability to be ​modest [in the scale ​of rate rises] has diminished”.

City analysts have interpreted the increasingly hawkish comments of Pill and other MPC members as making an interest rate rise in December almost inevitable. But there is disagreement about the strength of the economy, with many concerned that further increases in the cost of borrowing will hit the manufacturing sector and the construction industry, which has contracted for much of the year.

Households are also likely to cut back on spending in the new year, when the energy price cap is expected to rise to almost £2,000 for a typical home and council tax bills increase by an average of almost 5%.

How could the Nvidia CEO’s affair threaten US national security?

Published 13 November 2026

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of high-spec AI chips, as the fallout from the Nvidia scandal widens to President Donald Trump's cabinet.

Pressure is building on Lutnick from across the political spectrum to explain his department's actions.

Jensen Huang was ousted as Nvidia CEO after revelations he had an affair with a businesswoman who was also allegedly a Chinese spy.

Megaspeed, the firm she worked for, had been probed by US government agencies over suspicions it was smuggling Nvidia chips into China, reports said, but was not on a list of firms US companies are prevented from working with.

Bessent told CNBC several agencies "were in favour of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months".

"But Commerce has the pen... and you will have to ask them about their internal process," he added.

Bessent's comments come after Lutnick was called to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next month over the Commerce Department's role in allowing Nvidia to export its advanced chips.

Other congressional committees have asked both Lutnick and his department to retain all records relating to Nvidia and Huang.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said some parts of the administration wanted more controls on trade with Megaspeed

Bessent said he was "frustrated" by delays in putting the company on the export control list and reports of leakage of AI chips into China.

"President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s, so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, because it gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Last year, the Commerce Department had been investigating Megaspeed over suspicions it had been smuggling some of Nvidia's advanced AI chips into China, according to the New York Times. Megaspeed has been contacted for comment.

There was also pressure on the Commerce Department to add it to the list, but the Financial Times separately reported that the department was delaying efforts to have the cloud computing firm included.

However, Bessent also pointed the finger at Nvidia.

"The story has been thus far of Jensen Huang's personal foibles," he told CNBC , external .

"The real story here should be: did Nvidia know their client, and was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they were selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies?

"It's important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that."

Bessent's pointed comments are a rare instance of internal debate within the Trump administration spilling out into the public view, although tensions have reportedly simmered between Bessent and Lutnick in the past.

In 2024, the two reportedly jostled for the role of treasury secretary ahead of Trump's return to the White House, and last year the pair butted heads over the administration's tariff policy, according to US media.

How AI visionary Jensen Huang was undone by his own bad decisions Published 3 days ago

Huang has been summoned to testify before the Senate Banking Committee about his alleged affair with the former Megaspeed executive, who is suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The commerce secretary has also been summoned to appear before the committee in December.

"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," committee chairman Republican Senator Tim Scott posted on X.

Democrats on key congressional committees have asked the Commerce Department and Lutnick to keep all records relating to decisions to allow Nvidia to sell its advanced AI chips to Chinese companies, including all their communications with or about Nvidia and Huang.

Ways and Means Committee Ranking Member Richard E Neal and Senate Finance Committee Ranking Member Ron Wyden are starting investigations into the way Nvidia was allowed to sell these chips.

They say Nvidia's advanced H200 chips could be sold to Chinese firms if they were first imported from their manufacturing facility in Taiwan into the US for inspection.

A 25% tariff - a levy paid by US importers to the federal government - was imposed on those chips under a section of the Trade Act that Neal and Wyden say is meant to allow the US president to take action against imports that risk national security.

"Trump's use of the statute appears to have done the opposite, undermining US national security and putting Americans at risk," they said.

stories.body:
Channel 4 has announced its decision to cancel the reality TV show Married at First Sight UK (Mafs UK). It is the show that saw couples matched by relationship experts who were then wed in faux commitment ceremonies upon meeting for the first time.

The cancellation is the result of a BBC Panorama investigation in May 2026 which drew, among other sources, upon research by myself and colleagues at ReCARETV . Our project comprises more than 120 interviews with broadcasting executives, commissioners, production workers and reality TV participants.

The Panorama investigation highlighted accounts from former Mafs UK participants who came forward to journalists and our research team with allegations of sexual assault and misconduct during production. Even with strict anonymity protections in place, many still found it difficult to speak to us. Often, reality television participants do not realise that signing a confidentiality clause does not legally prevent them from speaking out about harm.

Change happens when people are finally heard and believed. Yet this places enormous pressure on already traumatised people to articulate their experiences and fit their narratives into available avenues for complaint. Having listened to these accounts, and heard their fears that others will suffer the same harm, Channel 4’s decision to end the show is a welcome step.

Yet, I wonder how that decision to cancel Mafs UK can be squared with the findings of Channel 4’s external reviews . Shared with the public on November 5, the reports found that the show did not break Ofcom’s broadcasting code and that it could “reasonably continue” with some extra measures in place.

For someone who experienced severe harm during production, waiting for Channel 4’s reports only to hear that the broadcaster’s practices met expected standards is potentially re-traumatising. Learning that the show could have continued would have made this harder to bear.

Compliance and responsibility

My ReCARETV colleagues and I have spent the last three years researching care in reality and unscripted TV production (our final report From Compliance to Care, is forthcoming). To us, it is not surprising that the show’s protocols were found to be compliant with the code.

This demonstrates that an emphasis on protocols, compliance and robust paperwork is not enough to protect people from harm. Our research shows that the realities of television production – specifically a fast-paced drive for drama and the conditions of a precarious, freelance workforce – frequently undermine these intentions.

The reasonable measures that are mentioned in the external review of Mafs UK for Channel 4 include installing CCTV in all rooms, the use of safe words and extra lockable bolts on bedrooms and bathrooms, among other suggestions which aim to take the pressure off the risks of intimacy.

Presumably, if Channel 4’s decision is still to cancel the show, this is because Mafs UK is now either too difficult to make, or changes would sufficiently diminish its popularity.

It seems that these responses to compliance and new safety measures disavow any acknowledgement that the show’s high pressure in production around sexual intimacy was essentially unsafe. Once again the TV industry is resisting any reasonable understanding of harm and reinforcing the exceptionalism of TV as a space where boundaries are pushed in the interests of creative freedom.

Ofcom’s response

Ofcom’s response after waiting for the Channel 4 reviews has been to offer more guidance to which broadcasters should “have regard”. These include some welcome considerations such as a more developed model of ongoing consent, allowing participants some access to family and friends away from the show and ensuring that background checks are completed in time.

These are all recommendations my research colleagues and I welcome and are supported by findings in our data that were shared with Ofcom over the summer. But the Ofcom guidance also introduces something new which is the mention of the “conduct” of participants. Our research suggests that participants are regularly issued codes of conduct on reality shows and the external Channel 4 report suggests heavier sanctions for participants breaking such codes. This sends a message about participants’ own responsibility.

Our research shows a major flaw in how duty-of-care compliance is sometimes built. Too often, it becomes a tick-box exercise designed to shield broadcasters from complaints, rather than protect participants from harm.

The ReCARETV research found that a common practice in reality TV is the so-called “talk of doom”, in which mental health professionals warn participants of worst-case scenarios to secure their consent. Rather than helping contributors understand how production and editing actually work, this approach shifts responsibility from the broadcaster onto the individual. Similarly, our concern with how the industry and regulators have responded to the trauma on Mafs UK is that they disperse responsibility for the harm, rather than owning it directly.

Ofcom, as a post-broadcast regulator, cannot offer any compensation to participants even if their complaint is upheld. There is still no formal space to protect participants who take part in reality shows.

Read more: How unions could help reality TV cast and crew win better pay and working conditions

My research colleagues and I welcome the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority , which is now formally recognised in Parliament as the independent whistleblowing body for film, TV, music and theatre – and the first to formally recognise reality TV participants within the creative industries. Still, change cannot rely only on people speaking out. The industry must also confront its own systemic failures and accept ethical responsibility.

The question should not just be about whether a show is compliant, but whether it is ethical, safe and humane.

stories.body:
Reporting Highlights

A Brutal Attack : A rookie cop in rural Alabama told his colleague he had hit his pregnant wife in the stomach and choked her before she started to miscarry.

Laws for the Unborn: Under Alabama law, fetuses have equal protections. But those laws are limited in how they punish people who abuse their pregnant partners.

Unequal Outcomes: Women accused of drug use during pregnancy face far more legal scrutiny, even when their babies are healthy.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital.

Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.

The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.

When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container.

“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.

Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family.

“Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.”

Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground.

“I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.”

According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.”

In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences.

The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder.

But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell.

His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.

In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison.

A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.

Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court.

“During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”

As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said.

Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital.

“If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email.

Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion.

“Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.”

Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.

“I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.

She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.

About a week before she went to the authorities, she got a text from her husband asking if she’d give him one more chance. “I can’t give you your baby back,” he wrote. “That’s something I’m always going to live with knowing I did that.”

Asked about the text, Robert wrote to ProPublica, “I was referring to having to pull my kid out a toilet I couldn’t believe I had to do that. It was painful emotionally.”

Robert had started working as an officer at the Headland Police Department about four months earlier. Brittany worried the other officers would side with her husband, but she quashed her fears and reached out on social media to several of them anyway. She said Robert went into her account and deleted the messages she’d sent. But it was too late.

Knight, one of the officers she messaged, confronted Robert, who admitted that he had hit Brittany in the stomach before the miscarriage, the officer later told the Dothan police. Robert furiously messaged Brittany.

“If you want me to go to jail keep accusing me of it,” he wrote. “Just know I love you and it will never happen again but I think I’m getting fired.”

Domestic abuse is a leading killer of pregnant women. And for every fatal case, there are an estimated 70 nonfatal ones. Researchers have found that almost 13% of women surveyed experienced domestic violence during pregnancy.

Nonfatal cases usually go unreported, according to Maeve Wallace, an expert on domestic violence at the University of Arizona. The same goes for miscarriages, which often happen at home and may leave no medical record. That can make it difficult to determine how often abuse causes miscarriage, she said.

Read More

Brittany said her relationship with Robert had been turbulent from the start. She was still in high school when they started dating, and she uprooted her life to relocate to his hometown of Dothan. She said he started physically hurting her months into the relationship and that it escalated after the move. Brittany found herself isolated in Alabama, where life revolved almost entirely around her husband, two young children and the couple’s car-detailing business.

“Robert would also hurt me if things weren’t done perfectly or if any issues happened,” Brittany wrote.

Unlike many other victims of domestic violence, she hounded the police and prosecutors to take her case seriously after the miscarriage.

Cases against abusers accused of causing pregnancy loss can be tricky to prove, often requiring evidence that the abuser intentionally struck the victim in the stomach and testimony from a forensic pathologist linking the violence to the pregnancy loss. In one strange turn, a grand jury in a city outside of Birmingham indicted a woman for starting a fight that led to her being shot in the stomach and suffering a miscarriage.

It’s easier and more common to pursue charges against defendants when they are accused of killing both a pregnant woman and her fetus.

Laws don’t provide an easy path for punishing abusers of pregnant women, especially when the baby survives, according to law professor Mary Ziegler, who teaches at the University of California, Davis. But laws do make prosecution of pregnant women who use drugs astonishingly easy. Those cases come to light almost automatically — and there is little opportunity to challenge them. Hospitals frequently administer drug tests to pregnant women and notify child protective services of positive results. Those agencies often turn over that information to police in Alabama, where drug use is not grounds just for a child welfare investigation but for a felony charge.

The women are prosecuted under Alabama’s chemical endangerment law, which makes it illegal to expose children to drugs. Although the 2006 law initially was designed to address the dangers of home-based meth labs, prosecutors almost immediately began using it against pregnant women.

ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County since 2009 on chemical endangerment charges after testing positive for drugs. An analysis of court data also found that the county prosecuted women for chemical endangerment at one of the highest rates in the state, though the data doesn’t specify whether the cases involved pregnancies.

In one case, a 24-year-old whose newborn tested positive for methadone and marijuana received a five-year prison sentence in 2009. Another woman, who’d been convicted for exposing her fetus to THC in 2013, had her probation revoked for possessing synthetic marijuana and spent about nine months in prison.

Pat Jones, who was Houston County’s district attorney at the time of these cases, did not respond to a request for comment.

According to Ziegler, there is a pronounced unevenness in who gets punished under statutes that protect fetuses.

“The versions of personhood that are enshrined in our laws have tended to focus on the conduct of women,” she said.

Courtney Haney grew up in Dothan but left at age 18 to join a high-pressure sales crew that traveled across the country, selling boxes of frozen meat door-to-door. The work was stressful, and it attracted misfits and risk-takers. Several of her colleagues used drugs, but Haney became pregnant unexpectedly and stayed clean.

Her daughter was born healthy, arriving exactly on her due date. But soon, cracks appeared in her relationship with the father, and he split, taking the baby with him. When her colleagues moved on to other cities, Haney remained in Denver to look for her child. She had no family there and no friends. Her despair became overwhelming. She turned to drugs and became homeless, eventually losing custody.

Almost a year later, Haney found out she was pregnant again and returned to Dothan in 2020 with a full-blown addiction to heroin. She went to the hospital with contractions the week before she gave birth and knew she would test positive for drugs. She also said no one offered her options for drug treatment, even after she asked for help. Instead, hospital staff stabilized and discharged her. She kept using until she returned to give birth, when she was drug-tested again.

“I was holding my daughter in my hands and the police walked in,” Haney said.

They asked her questions, and she hoped they might show mercy and allow her to go home with her child. After they told her she might be charged with a felony for exposing her fetus to drugs, she burst into tears.

“I answered honestly, thinking that if I’ve answered honestly they wouldn’t press charges,” she said. “And that was pointless.”

She was arrested for chemical endangerment three months later.

For women struggling with addiction during pregnancy, a chemical endangerment arrest can initiate a cycle of devastating court fees, imprisonment on probation violations and even additional charges. And the separation from their newborns and other children can drive them deeper into addiction. Unlike in many other counties, Houston County does not offer a drug court program, which allows defendants to get substance-abuse treatment instead of prison time and avoid a felony on their record.

A woman who was about seven months’ pregnant was arrested in Houston County the very same day as Robert Maddox, in 2022. She was briefly jailed for violating probation stemming from a past chemical endangerment conviction. She then faced additional felony charges when, weeks later, she tested positive for cocaine at the hospital where she gave birth. She later received a five-year sentence and wound up at Tutwiler Prison for Women.

Her release date is right before Christmas in 2028.

Haney had no felony convictions, but a sentencing report recommended against straight probation due to charges in other states that had been dismissed. Ultimately, the Houston County district attorney’s office offered a plea deal for a lesser charge and just over a year of probation.

Haney struggled to abide by the conditions of her sentence. She did not complete court-ordered drug treatment and failed to report to her probation officer several times. As a result, she was jailed for a total of four months.

Many of the other women jailed with her also had been arrested on charges of chemical endangerment as a result of failing drug tests during childbirth.

“Whenever I went to jail, that’s where I met most of them,” Haney said. “There’s a whole lot of them in Houston County.”

Haney became pregnant two more times while she was addicted. For her third child, she traveled to nearby Georgia to give birth, and then to Florida for her fourth. Neither state arrests women for prenatal drug use at the same high rate as Alabama.

Xaviera Smith, a former nurse and mother of three from Tennessee, said she knew she would be arrested before she even gave birth in Houston County to her youngest son in 2018. Smith couldn’t deny the results of the drug test that had been administered while she was in labor. She had been battling a meth addiction for years.

She said that, fortunately, her baby was born healthy and did not need to go to the neonatal intensive care unit for drug withdrawal.

Smith had a court-appointed attorney who negotiated a deal on her chemical endangerment charge. She was sentenced to 10 years but could avoid prison by serving time through the local work-release program.

“I just went to court and took what they gave me,” Smith said. ”There’s nothing I really could do.”

After violating the terms of work release, she ended up in prison for nearly a year.

Brittany Maddox believed the case against her husband was a straightforward one. She felt there was solid evidence that the abuse caused her miscarriage. But the effort proved to be harder than she anticipated.

A few months after his arrest, the grand jury declined to indict him for murder, opting instead for a lesser charge of manslaughter.

The indictment alleged that Robert had “recklessly” caused the death of his wife’s fetus by “punching her in the stomach with a closed fist.” The maximum punishment would be 20 years in prison.

As Robert waited for his day in court, he asked the judge to relax some of the conditions of his bond. He had lost his job with the Headland police because of his wife’s claims of abuse and had started washing cars again. He wanted the court to remove the ankle monitor so he could more easily travel to work in Florida, which is near Dothan.

From her home out of state, Brittany had been calling the district attorney’s office once or twice a month to ensure authorities kept an eye on her estranged husband’s whereabouts. She was shocked to learn of his out-of-state travel request — not from prosecutors but from a news story. For the first time since his arrest, she felt unsafe.

A judge denied his motion to remove the ankle monitor but granted his request to commute to north Florida.

Brittany stayed in touch with prosecutors and began to mentally prepare for trial. She said that as months stretched into years, the conversations with them began to shift. They asked her how she felt about a plea deal, and she said she would be open to it, as long as the charge related to her miscarriage wasn’t dropped completely.

“I told them I could push through a trial emotionally,” Brittany wrote.

Finally, almost four years after Robert was arrested, his attorney brokered a plea deal with prosecutors. He would plead guilty to domestic violence, and the prosecution would recommend the manslaughter charge be dismissed.

Goodman, the district attorney, told ProPublica that he would not have been able to prove at trial that Robert committed manslaughter. “There was never any evidence that tied the actions of the defendant to the death of the baby,” he said, adding that “no expert could tie a causal connection.”

He also said he explained to Brittany that “we would not have moved forward on the manslaughter case” had he been in office when his predecessor chose to seek an indictment against Robert.

Brittany said if Goodman believed the charge should be dropped, he should have done it sooner, instead of having her spend years preparing for trial.

“The charge being dropped four years after he was arrested as part of a plea deal makes no sense to me,” she said. “That wrecked me in a lot of ways, more than the times I laid in bed for days after he hurt me.”

On May 18, 2026, Robert appeared before a judge in a Houston County courtroom. Brittany attended the hearing as well. She had traveled to Alabama for all of the hearings, even though she still feared being in the same room with Robert.

After all that waiting, the sentencing felt surprisingly short to her. When the judge moved to dismiss the most serious charge, he didn’t say the word manslaughter or mention the miscarriage. Brittany said she tried to ask questions about the deal, but she wasn’t sworn in, and the judge quickly moved on.

“The victim and the defendant were in a verbal dispute whereas the defendant was alleged to throw the victim down and choke her,” the judge said. “The state alleges that this occurred in front of their minor children as well.”

The judge went on to say that the presence of the children might have increased Robert’s punishment to a minimum six months’ imprisonment. But because he was a first-time offender, that minimum didn’t apply.

The judge sentenced him to five years’ probation and fined him about $3,000, which he could pay off at $50 a month. Then the judge added one more thing: anger management classes, to be completed through the court referral office.
